variations.subject: Keep the War Memorial to honour our fallen
variations.body:
Dear Minister,

I am writing about the plans for the Australian War Memorial.

The Memorial is not a political vehicle. It is our national shrine, the resting place of the record of 103,000 Australians who died serving the Commonwealth. It must not be used for activism or contested history.

I ask you to do three things:

1. Keep the Memorial to honour Australian troops who died serving the Commonwealth of Australia, as per its charter.
2. Describing the frontier conflicts as a war is activist revision. Involving contested history like this dishonours our fallen.
3. Ensure activist or contested history never features in the Memorial.

The heritage review closing 30 September is the chance for Australians to be heard on this.

I would appreciate a response setting out your position.

Yours sincerely,

issue.heading: A shrine, not a soapbox.
issue.lede: A $550 million works programme is converting Australia's national shrine into an activist billboard, rewriting what it says about Australia and our fallen.
issue.proseHeading: Our shrine is NOT for politics or activism.
prose: The Memorial was built to one purpose: to hold the record of Australians who died serving the Commonwealth. Charles Bean called it the grave they never had. For 85 years, governments of both stripes kept faith with that purpose.

That has changed. Under the works programme, exhibition floor space is being multiplied, curatorial plans introduce frontier conflict displays and "contested history" framing, and the ground beneath the Parade Ground has been excavated. None of it was ever put to Australians as a whole. Until 30 September, it finally is.

Make no mistake about why. The activists pushing these changes want to delegitimise Australia and the fact of its settlement, and the nation's shrine is the most sacred platform they can seize for that cause.

notAWar.heading: The frontier conflicts were not a war.
body: Describing the frontier conflicts as a war is activist revision, not history. We reject the false history and narrative that this country was engaged in a widespread frontier war.

In reality, Australia was settled relatively peacefully compared with other countries: research so far suggests only seven British soldiers were killed during Australia's colonisation. Contested claims like these belong in museums and history books, not in the nation's shrine.

about.heading: Ordinary Australians.
about.lede: Veterans, families of the fallen, and people who simply stood at a dawn service once and understood what the quiet was for.
who: Defend Sacred Ground began around kitchen tables in Canberra and grew through RSL halls, veterans' groups, and families with a name on the Roll of Honour. We hold no office, take no party's money, and want nothing for ourselves.

We want one thing: that the Australian War Memorial remains what it was built to be, a place that honours Australians who died serving the Commonwealth, free of activism and contested history. When the plans are withdrawn, this campaign winds itself up.

directors.name: Roger Karge
directors.bio: Researcher and editor best known for the Dark Emu Exposed project, which tests popular claims about Australian history against the primary record. Roger runs the campaign's operations and keeps its claims anchored to evidence.

directors.name: Peter O'Brien
directors.bio: Army veteran and writer. Peter drafted the campaign's statement and plan, and leads its dealings with parliamentarians of every party who believe the Memorial should stay above politics.

directors.name: Robert Hill
directors.bio: Author of the campaign's manifesto, The Australian War Memorial Is Not a Frontier Conflict Museum: frontier history belongs in history, and the Memorial belongs to those who served Australia.
